answers.text:
In this article, superposition is the strategy of packing more features into a neural network than it has neurons, by giving up on composition (combining independent features together) and instead storing many separate, unrelated things in the same set of neurons, relying on a non-linear step to pull any one of them back out.

The clearest illustration in the piece is the "highly-distributed" code, where dense codes can represent far more, totally unrelated objects than there are neurons, but it becomes impossible to generically pick out most colors or shapes with a simple linear read, or to represent anything "in between" two categories. The article stresses that this only works if the underlying features don't compose: the code switches back to using whole (color, shape) pairs rather than independent color and shape features, because maximal superposition is only possible if there isn't composition.

The reason this matters, and why Olah keeps contrasting it with composition, is that the two are treated as competing ways of using the same limited "space" a network has to represent things. As the article puts it, if you have a fixed number of bits, features that compose freely need exponentially more room, so you can only store fully composable features that way; but if there's no composition, you can instead store an exponential number of separate items in superposition, at the cost of needing a non-linearity to retrieve them. Later the note softens this into a spectrum rather than an all-or-nothing choice: when features are sparse (rarely co-occurring), the unused "gaps" left by limited composition can themselves be filled with other features stored in superposition, as in Thorpe's "semi-distributed" example where the code puts the color features in mutual superposition, and the shapes in mutual superposition, while still composing color and shape together.

Superposition here is the same idea Olah's team already works with in their earlier "Toy Models of Superposition" research, just described from the neuroscience angle Thorpe used, rather than in terms of feature sparsity.

answers.asked: An informal note on the relationship between superposition and distributed representations by Chris Olah.
answers.text:
This is the article's own subtitle, naming the author and giving a one-line description of what the piece is about. The two things worth unpacking are who is writing it and what the two technical terms in the title mean, since both get defined properly only later in the piece.

Chris Olah is a Canadian machine learning researcher and a co-founder of Anthropic, known for his work on neural network interpretability, particularly mechanistic interpretability, and for research and tools that visualise internal representations in neural networks. Before Anthropic, he left Google Brain to lead OpenAI's interpretability team, then left OpenAI and co-founded Anthropic a year later. He's also credited with coining the term "mechanistic interpretability" itself, and this note is published on Anthropic's "Transformer Circuits Thread," the venue where he and colleagues publish this kind of interpretability research.

"Superposition" and "distributed representations" are the two ideas the whole piece is built around, and the note is explicit that it's trying to untangle them rather than treat them as the same thing: as the introduction puts it, it seems to the authors that "distributed representations" might be understood as containing two different ideas, which they call "composition" and "superposition," and these two different notions have very different properties in terms of generalization and what functions can be linearly computed from them. So the subtitle you selected is really flagging the article's whole argument in miniature: distributed representations is a familiar term from neuroscience and connectionist AI, and this note argues that superposition (packing more features than you have neurons, decodable only nonlinearly) is a distinct, competing strategy from composition (independent features combining linearly), even though both get called "distributed."

The "informal note" framing matters too: the piece explains later on that informal notes allow us to publish ideas that aren't as refined and developed as a full paper, and mistakes are very possible — so it's being pitched as a working reflection rather than a polished research paper.

answers.asked: What does "superposition" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In this piece, "superposition" names a strategy for packing more features into a layer than it has neurons, by letting neurons take on more than one meaning (being "polysemantic") rather than each neuron standing for one thing. Olah introduces it through Thorpe's "highly distributed" code, where a representation of colored shapes uses only 4 neurons — as many combinations as 4 bits can hold, "just as 4 bits can represent 16 numbers" — and calls this "maximal superposition" [spya-bzhkhu]. The cost is that you lose the ability to read features straight off with a simple linear check: Dense codes like this have a very cool advantage: they can represent far more, totally unrelated objects than there are neurons. But note that there are also lots of costs to this. It isn't possible to generically select most colors or shapes with a linear probe, let alone sets. Retrieving what's stored requires passing the representation through a non-linearity rather than just reading a direction off it, as the piece puts it when contrasting it with composition: If one has \(m\) bits to encode stimuli, we can think of there as being \(\exp(m)\) volume. Storing \(n\) features which arbitrarily compose together requires \(\exp(n)\) volume; so we can only store fully composable features in \(m\) bits. But if there's no composition, one can instead store \(\exp(m)\) items in superposition, although a non-linearity is required to retrieve them.

Why it matters to the argument: the whole piece is built around separating superposition from the other thing people also call a "distributed representation," namely composition — building objects out of independent features (like separate "color" and "shape" neurons combining) [spya-qcd003 spya-xcdtte]. Olah's claim is that these are not two points on one "local-to-distributed" spectrum, as Thorpe's framing might suggest, but two orthogonal, competing strategies for spending the same fixed budget of representational "volume": That is, composition and superposition are two different ways to allocate the exponential volume. Because they compete, a representation can't have unlimited amounts of both — composition buys you features that generalize and can be read off linearly, while superposition buys you the ability to store exponentially more items than you have neurons, at the cost of losing that easy linear readability. Superposition only becomes possible where composition is limited, i.e. where feature combinations are sparse rather than dense, since dense combinations force one feature per neuron [spya-qbuyka spya-ajbh7f]. This distinction is the reason the piece cares about it at all: understanding whether a network's representations decompose into a linear number of composable features versus needing exponential search through superposed, entangled ones is treated as central to being able to reverse-engineer neural networks at all [spya-v47ca7 spya-nwuh77].

"Monosemantic" here means having a single, fixed meaning — a neuron that stands for exactly one thing. In the passage, it describes the "local code," where there's a neuron for each (shape, color) pair, and this model "doesn't have any superposition." So each neuron is dedicated to one specific shape-color combination (say, "red circle"), rather than being shared across multiple, unrelated concepts.

The word is chosen in deliberate contrast to "polysemantic," which the note uses later for neurons that respond to several different features at once, as in the case of the "semi-distributed" code where units "begin to have some meaning – they're polysemantic, but only respond to a few features." A monosemantic neuron, then, is the opposite extreme: clean, single-purpose, and easy to interpret on its own, but — as the surrounding passage goes on to point out — wasteful, since it takes one neuron per possible combination rather than letting neurons do double duty.

This vocabulary of "monosemantic" versus "polysemantic" comes from the broader interpretability work Chris Olah and colleagues have done on superposition, where the central puzzle is that real neural network neurons are often polysemantic (mixing many features together) rather than monosemantic, which makes them harder to decode individually.

answers.asked: In our language, this model is "monosemantic" and doesn't have any superposition.
answers.text:
"Monosemantic" here means each neuron stands for exactly one thing and one thing only. In the local code just described, there's a separate neuron for every possible (shape, color) pair — one neuron just for "red circle," a different one just for "blue square," and so on. Since each neuron never does double duty, it has a single, clean meaning: that's what "monosemantic" is naming.

"Superposition" is the article's term for a network cramming more features into its neurons than it has neurons to spare, by letting neurons take on multiple overlapping meanings at once so that features share directions rather than each getting its own. Because this local code has enough neurons to give every single combination its own dedicated neuron, it never needs to do that kind of compression — hence "doesn't have any superposition."

The sentence is setting up the rest of the passage: this local code is described as wasteful precisely because it avoids superposition by brute force, using one neuron per combination rather than packing multiple combinations into shared neurons. The two codes discussed right after it — the "semi-local" and "highly-distributed" codes — are the article's examples of the alternative strategies (composition and superposition, respectively) that let a network use fewer neurons than this monosemantic scheme requires.

answers.asked: What does "monosemantic" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In this piece, "monosemantic" describes a neuron that stands for exactly one thing — it fires for a single (shape, color) pairing and nothing else, as in the "local code" example where there's a dedicated neuron for each shape-color combination, a setup the author says "is 'monosemantic' and doesn't have any superposition" [spya-kcjqdw]. So here "monosemantic" is just the flip side of superposition: a neuron that represents one feature cleanly, with no other feature packed into the same neuron.

Why it matters to the argument: this local code is the baseline case the whole piece builds from. It's wasteful — a neuron for every combination — but because each neuron means exactly one thing, the representation is maximally easy to interpret, and the author notes it has some surprisingly strong properties, like being able to represent arbitrary sets of stimuli and supporting very flexible linear readout [spya-hbmajb]. Starting from this monosemantic, no-superposition case sets up the contrast that structures the rest of the note: composition (the "semi-local" code) keeps this one-feature-per-neuron property while using independent neurons for color and shape that combine, whereas superposition (the "dense" code) gives up monosemanticity to pack more features into fewer neurons, at the cost of losing clean linear readout [spya-c2eewa spya-xwq6ty]. The concept of monosemanticity is what lets the author later argue that superposition is fundamentally in tension with easy interpretability, since interpretability depends on being able to point to what a neuron or direction represents [spya-armg2f spya-v47ca7].
